```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE)
```

`fit()` runs a chain of stages (preburn, burn, adapt, sample) and stops each one when its
stop rule is met or its try budget is used up. For most models that is all you need. For
hard fits — many subjects with a few extreme ones, race models with many effects on rates,
DDMs with across-trial variability — `hardfit()` runs the same sampler under a stricter
stop rule, watches for chains that have gone wrong, stops early when a fit will not
converge, and records how the fit ended. `diagnose()` reads that record, or any fitted
object, and says which of five outcomes you are looking at and what to do about it.

## What "converged" means in hardfit()

A fit is converged when, on the kept sample-stage draws, all of the following hold:

1. **Rhat.** The split-Rhat of every group-level parameter, and the `.99` quantile of the
   Rhats of all subject-level parameters, is below 1.1. This is the classical check: the
   chains agree on where the posterior is. With hundreds of subjects the plain maximum is set
   by one subject's worst parameter, so the rule reads the top 1% instead. For
   `type = "single"` the rule is the maximum over the subject's parameters at 1.05.
2. **Effective sample size.** The smallest effective sample size over the group means and the
   log group standard deviations, summed over chains, is at least 100. Rhat below 1.1 can be
   reached with 30–60 effective draws, which puts the Monte Carlo error of a posterior median
   near a tenth of a posterior SD; 100 is the point beyond which more draws changed no
   posterior summary in the fits we checked, and 200 roughly halves how many fits stop.
3. **No chain in a different region.** The chains' summed subject log-likelihoods lie within
   100 units of each other. Two chains with the same Rhat on the parameters but a likelihood
   gap of hundreds of units are in different regions of the posterior, usually one of them
   degenerate.
4. **No subject in a different region.** For every subject, the chains' median log-likelihoods
   for that subject lie within 15 units. A subject whose chains disagree by more than that has
   two posterior modes, which the group-level Rhat cannot see.

The first criterion is the one that binds in almost every hard fit; the other three are
safety nets that never fire when the chains agree, and each catches a case the Rhat alone
passes.

Independently of the stop rule, **culling** watches for a chain that has drifted into a
degenerate region: a chain whose likelihood is more than 200 units below the best chain's
(and more than 5 within-chain spreads), for two checks running, and either more than 1,000
below or also lower on its own log posterior, has its state replaced by a copy of a healthy
chain's. The check runs at every burn check, once more at the end of burn-in, and at every
sample-stage check. Replacing a chain's state during burn-in is a change of starting point
and does not alter the posterior; a replacement in the sample stage restarts the kept draws.

Finally, an **early stop**: a fit whose rule Rhat is still above 1.5 at the 20th sample-stage
check is ended there and marked as aborted. Of 46 fits in that position (hierarchical and
single-subject), none met the rule later, so continuing them spends compute for nothing.

## Running a hard fit

```{r}
emc <- make_emc(data, design, n_chains = 6)
emc <- hardfit(emc)
```

Six chains rather than three roughly halves the chance that a two-mode subject goes
unnoticed, and give the chain replacement healthy chains to copy from; `hardfit()` prints a
note when a hierarchical object has fewer. The defaults are the four criteria above, culling
on, the early stop at Rhat 1.5 and check 20, and 40 checks of 100 draws per stage (`fit()`'s
default is 20). Every threshold is an argument, and `NULL` turns a criterion off:

```{r}
emc <- hardfit(emc, max_gd = 1.1, gd_quantile = .99, min_ess = 100, max_ll_gap = 100,
               max_subj_spread = 15, cull = TRUE, abort_gd = 1.5, abort_try = 20,
               max_tries = 40, iter = 1000, step_size = 100)
```

`hardfit()` drives the same sampler as `fit()` one check at a time, so a fit started with
`fit()` can be continued with `hardfit()` and the reverse; the kernel adapted during warm-up
is kept either way.

## Reading the progress line

Each sample-stage check prints one line:

```
[sample | try=7 | iters=700 | Rhat=2.072 (rule; max 11.310) | min ESS=47 (v_CIcong) |
 LL gap=56 | subject spread=15.6 (s353; 6 > 5)] Duration: 47.1 s - ETA (to max_tries): 25.9 min
```

- `Rhat=2.072 (rule; max 11.310)`: the value the stop rule compares with 1.1, and the plain
  maximum over every parameter. When the two differ by this much, one subject is far from
  the others; the rule has put it in the top 1% and is reading the rest.
- `min ESS=47 (v_CIcong)`: the smallest effective sample size and its parameter. The parameter
  tells you where the mixing is slow: here a rate effect, typically the direction along which
  the chains disagree.
- `LL gap=56`: the largest difference between chains in summed log-likelihood. Healthy fits
  sit under 40; the veto is 100; a cull needs 200.
- `subject spread=15.6 (s353; 6 > 5)`: the subject with the widest disagreement between
  chains, its spread in log-likelihood units, and how many subjects exceed 5. Subject s353
  here has two modes and the chains have split between them.

A cull prints on the line of the check it happened at:

```
... | chain 2 respawned from chain 5 (log-likelihood 8986 below, z = 74.7); sample stage restarted]
```

and the early stop as a warning naming the check, the value and the threshold.

## The record

After the sample stage the fit carries a record of how it ended:

```{r}
str(emc[[1]]$stop_record)
#> $ criteria: the thresholds that were on
#> $ met     : TRUE if every criterion passed on one set of draws
#> $ tries   : checks used (since the last restart)
#> $ rule    : the Rhat the stop rule read at the last check
#> $ stats   : ess_min, ess_min_par, rhat_b, rhat_ident, ll_gap, ll_z, ll_worst_chain,
#>             subj_spread, subj_spread_n5, subj_spread_subject, flat (the drift statistics below)
#> $ culls   : number of chains replaced (the list is emc[[1]]$culls)
#> $ discards: checks at which the first third was dropped (only when that met the rule)
#> $ aborted : NULL, or the check, value and threshold of an early stop
#> $ restarts: sample-stage restarts after a cull
#> $ trace   : one row per check: draws, rule, max Rhat, min ESS, LL gap, subject spread
#> $ previous: the record of an earlier hardfit() call on the same object
```

Two statistics in `stats` are not on the progress line and are the most useful for an
unmet fit:

- `rhat_b` is the Rhat of the draws projected on the direction along which the chain means
  differ most. It is close to the largest parameter Rhat and says how far apart the chains are.
- `rhat_ident` is the Rhat projected on the direction the posterior pins down most tightly,
  that is the combination of parameters the data identify best. If `rhat_ident` is near 1
  while `rhat_b` is large, the chains agree on everything the data determine and disagree
  only along a direction the data do not.

## diagnose()

```{r}
d <- diagnose(emc)
d
d$class
```

`diagnose()` works on any fitted object, whether or not it has a record, because it reads
the draws: the rule Rhat and the four statistics, a per-chain table (median summed
log-likelihood, gap to the best chain, whether the chain is lower on its own log posterior,
whether it would be culled), the per-subject spread, the drift statistics, and the class.

### The drift statistics

The record and `diagnose()` carry a second kind of diagnostic, which asks a different
question from Rhat and ESS: is the posterior location still *moving* during the sample
stage? For each of four series the draws of all chains are pooled, the first third is
compared with the last third, and the difference of medians is expressed in IQR units
("drift"), with the Monte Carlo error of that difference ("se"):

```
Drift (first vs last third, in IQRs; se): mu 0.60 (0.21), alpha 0.62 (0.25), LL 0.08 (0.05), subj_ll 0.14 (0.07)
```

- `mu`: the group-level means (maximum over parameters);
- `alpha`: the subject-level parameters (`.99` quantile over all of them);
- `LL`: the summed log-likelihood;
- `subj_ll`: the per-subject log-likelihoods (`.99` quantile).

A drift within about 3 of its se is noise. Rhat compares the chains with each other at the
same time, ESS measures how autocorrelated each chain is; the drift statistics would be the
only ones to notice all chains sliding together, along a ridge in the same direction, with
Rhat unaffected. In practice such a slide also makes the autocorrelation enormous, so the
ESS floor catches it first, and the drift statistics are reported rather than used as a
stop criterion. Their value is in reading an unmet fit. The pattern

```
LL 0.08 (0.05), subj_ll 0.14 (0.07)     stationary
mu 0.60 (0.21), alpha 0.62 (0.25)       moving
```

means the parameters are still drifting while the likelihood is not: the chains are moving
along a direction the likelihood is flat on. That is the ridge signature of outcome 4 below.
Drift in `LL` or `subj_ll` well beyond its se means a chain or a subject is still changing
region, outcome 5.

## Five outcomes, and what to do with each

### 1. `met`

```
met = TRUE, tries = 33, rule = 1.085, stats$ess_min = 133, ll_gap = 23, subj_spread = 3.1
```

Converged under every criterion. Use the fit. `culls > 0` here is harmless: a chain started
badly and was replaced early.

### 2. `ess_held`: Rhat passed, ESS short

```
met = FALSE, rule = 1.07, stats$ess_min = 54 (lsd:B), tries = 40
```

The old rule would have called this converged. The chains agree but the group SD of `B` has
only 54 effective draws, so its posterior median is known to about 0.17 posterior SDs.
Continue the fit:

```{r}
emc <- hardfit(emc)
```

A continuation adds another 1,000 draws per chain and re-checks. Expect ESS to grow roughly
with the draws (0.5–1.5 per 100 draws per chain in slow fits); once or twice is usually enough.

### 3. `aborted`

```
met = FALSE, aborted = list(try = 20, rule = 2.246, abort_gd = 1.5)
```

Do not continue it. Look at `rhat_ident` and the LL gap to decide which of the next two cases
it is, then act on the model or the start points, not the iteration count.

### 4. `ridge_only`

```
met = FALSE, tries = 40, rule = 1.23, stats: rhat_b = 2.22, rhat_ident = 1.006,
  ess_min = 31 (v_lMd), ll_gap = 28, subj_spread = 4.0,
  drift: mu 0.60 (0.21), alpha 0.62 (0.25), LL 0.08 (0.05), subj_ll 0.14 (0.07)
```

The chains agree on every identified quantity (`rhat_ident` near 1) and on the likelihood (gap
28, `LL` drift within noise), and are still moving along one direction (`mu` and `alpha`
drift three times their se). To see which direction, look at the within-chain correlations
of the group means:

```{r}
cor(t(emc[[1]]$samples$theta_mu[, emc[[1]]$samples$stage == "sample"]))
```

A pair at −0.99 or beyond is the ridge. In race models it is typically the rate intercept
against its match effect: the rate of the losing accumulator, which few errors leave almost
unidentified. The posterior along that direction is set by the prior, not the data, and no
amount of running will make six chains agree on it quickly.

What to do: report the identified quantities (sums or differences of the correlated pair,
and everything else, all of which have Rhat near 1) and say that the ridge direction is
prior-determined; or reparameterise so the identified combination is a parameter; or
tighten the prior on the weakly identified rate. Continuing helps only if the rule Rhat was
still falling at the last checks (`diagnose(emc)$falling`).

### 5. `region_mode`

```
met = FALSE, rule = 1.56, stats: rhat_ident = 1.56, ll_gap = 125,
  subj_spread = 15.4 (s254; 7 > 5), drift: LL 0.9 (0.1), subj_ll 2.4 (0.2)
```

The chains disagree on something the data identify, and the likelihood itself is still
moving (`LL` and `subj_ll` drift far beyond their se). Either a chain is in a worse region
(`ll_gap` large, `ll_worst_chain` names it) or one or more subjects have two modes
(`subj_spread` large, the subject named). For a subject with two modes, the chains that found
the better one have the higher subject log-likelihood; compare across seeds:

```{r}
fits <- list(hardfit(emc_a), hardfit(emc_b), hardfit(emc_c))   # three seeds
sapply(fits, function(f) sum(apply(f[[1]]$samples$subj_ll, 1, median)))
```

A seed whose summed log-likelihood sits ten or more units below the best is in a worse mode:
hold it and use the others. No stop rule or chain replacement can fix a case where most
chains sit in the worse mode; several seeds are the only reliable detector, and 6 chains
rather than 3 roughly halves the chance that a two-mode subject goes unnoticed.

### Unmet at `max_tries`, still falling

```
trace$rule at checks 20, 30, 40: 1.50, 1.42, 1.354
```

`diagnose()` reports `falling = TRUE` when the rule Rhat decreased over the last three
checks of an unmet fit. The fit is converging slowly: one continuation (at most two) is
worth it. If the Rhat rises under continuation instead, the problem is structural (case 4
or 5), not slow mixing.

## Grading a set of fits

With many fits, grade them from `diagnose()` rather than by eye:

```{r}
grades <- sapply(fits, function(f) diagnose(f)$class)
table(grades)
```

## What the diagnostics do not tell you

- A parameter whose posterior mean is several prior SDs from the prior mean is under
  tension between the prior and the likelihood; chains can sit for a long time on a shallow
  plateau between the two. Check `credible(emc)` against the prior means for any fit that is
  slow for no visible reason.
- A single chain can make a long excursion and come back; Rhat over a window can read 1.26
  where Rhat over the whole run reads 1.06. The stop rule reads all kept draws, discarding
  the first third only when that alone makes the stop pass, and records when it does.
- The two-mode check needs at least one chain in each mode. With 3 chains a two-mode subject
  goes undetected in a quarter to a third of runs; with 6, about one in ten.
